Perfume rating 4.18 out of 5 with 11,247 votes

Armani Code by Giorgio Armani is a Oriental Spicy fragrance for men. Armani Code was launched in 2004. The nose behind this fragrance is Antoine Lie. Top notes are Lemon and Bergamot; middle notes are Star Anise, Olive Blossom and Guaiac Wood; base notes are Leather, Tonka Bean and Tobacco. This perfume is the winner of award FiFi Award Fragrance Of The Year Men`s Luxe 2006 .

Tomasz K. 11/28/25 07:51

The creators intended for Code to be an intriguing and oriental fragrance, but it ended up being rather bland. The individual notes blend together into a vague and indistinct mix, lacking coherence. The scent is polite and predictable, without any surprising twists. It’s easily forgettable. There's no bold, masculine character here, leaving the fragrance feeling completely unremarkable. The composition seems designed primarily for what’s known as ‘blotter appeal’—something that smells nice on paper but lacks substance in real life. If this is meant to be a fragrance for men trying to seduce women, I doubt it will bring much success. In my opinion, Code is yet another example, like Bleu de Chanel, that proves the oriental olfactory style doesn't accommodate compromise. And if I had to choose between the two, I’d probably prefer Polge’s creation over Lie and Maisondieu's.

My rating: I discourage it. (2/7)

ljundia 07/12/25 08:08

Great smell in general, this was one of my first designer fragrances like 4 or 5 years ago when I wasn't into collecting, and just wanted a sexy and classy night all-rounder, I went with this one. Not super dark, it was some sweetness and brightness in the opening, but not sweetness like modern vanilla-tonka-amber accords, is kind of liquorice-like, and very 2000's, in my head it smells like a kind and easy-going dad in his late 30s or something, but it can really fit anyone over 20. In the dry-down is very classy and woody leather, but very close. Definitely masculine but not in a dark way but in a sexy, classy but not overtly formal, but you need to dress up a bit for wearing this imo.

The thing is, and needs to be said, this fragrance is a straight up fraud. And yes I mean performance-wise. It lasts a decent 4-5 hours, but the sillage becomes almost skin scent after 40 minutes or something. I remembering using like 8 or 9 sprays one night, I went out, after a few hours I was talking closely and dancing with a girl, then kissing, etc and it wasn't until she was literally on my neck, she went back a bit shocked and told me "hey you smell really good" like it was the first time she noticed after being close to her for hours. It has been reformuled now, I really don't like the iris twist on the new one but the performance on this was one of the things that made me look for other things and start in the fragrance world.

smellslikejustspirit 07/10/25 03:08

This is a perfectly unisex fragrance, I can't believe no-ones comparing these but it reminds me of a less minty, warmer version of Le Male Elixir. My god is this warm, sexy, and seductive on me. The citrus top note wears off fast and goes very mild, into an overlay of freshness, and the fragrance turns into a warm, spicy, and very mildly leathery scent. I can't believe there isn't a sugary/honey note in here because it turns really sweet and thick on my skin, but then that happens with a lot of frags for me. I think it's the vanilla base, and it's incredible. Thank god this is still a basic frag and the tobacco is more to show off the desired vibe through notes than any actual photorealistic tobacco, because tobacco makes me gag.

On a woman I think this is a very seductive, yet powerful scent, that is sweet, whilst holding it's ground. On a man I can imagine the sharpness and citrus coming out more, but being warmed up by the spice, and creating an alluring softness around the wearer. Personally I think on a man it will still have crowdpleaser DNA which isn't for me, but on women this is just the right amount of sexy, but original.

ShadowsofLight 02/13/25 11:21

A.C has such a classic, classy profile...and it's completely baked into it's DNA. It just *is* formal...because it...is. I'm struggling to describe it in any other terms.

My only issue is that the opening citruses on top of the suede-y leather is a tad rubbery until the initial 10 minutes pass after applying. I'm really not sure why this reads as *rubber* to my nose, but it does, and I've tested it on myself and paper 3 times.

It has a fresh blue muskiness as it settles...where is that coming from? It's not citruses. It's like a body wash scent combining with the smoothness of the tonka...so it's blue&clean+soft&powdery all at once. This fragrance is full-bodied.

Without the blueness (And seriously, who cares, it's 2025, wear what you like regardless of gender!) I would claim this is unisex, but it's classically masculine and I personally don't feel like it fits me (a woman in my 30s).

I've never smelled this in public (but it should be noted that I don't smell much out there anyway in my area), so I cannot relate to the complaints that this is "overworn". It has a nice balance of warm and cool tones, rendering it a useful and versatile fragrance for most seasons (maybe not high heat, but summer nights would be alright).

I will say, this is tasteful, and very pleasing. Nothing challenging, but interesting nonetheless. If I smelled this on the street, I'd definitely look around to see who was wearing it.

mkpunk 12/27/24 07:46

The classic Armani Code is still available on eBay and it still smells like Armani Code. I have own three smell alikes of Armani Code and after getting Armani Code Parfum, I knew I had to get Armani Code. I own Bath and Body Works Noir (classic bottle), Sean John and La Rive Password. All are good in some way but miss facets of Armani Code.

Armani Code opens with lemon and some bergamot. I want to say all the clones have various degrees of citrus in the open. The mid is a mix of spice from the star anise and a slight smokiness from the guaiac wood with some tobacco seeping in with the spice and smoke. The base adds leather and tonka to the tobacco.

None of the clones I own have the smokiness of Armani Code. None are leathery though Noir is seemingly animalic in a clean way (think Drakkar Noir.) Sean John is clean and the closest performance wise. La Rive missed the mark and it smells more like the boxing time traveler version of newer Armani Code and Armani Code Parfum replacing iris with violet. That said, it still fits the Armani Code wheelhouse enough to smell similar.

I live in AZ so this fall/winter night scent is only worn sparingly. I can see it used for concerts and going to bars. I wouldn't suggest dates since it has been around long enough it is if not a brother scent maybe a dad scent for college aged kids. I can't comment on the new bottle fitting that as they changed the notes quite a bit.

Overall I loved this DNA before I knew it. I am glad I got the original while they still circulate through the retailers and resellers. I rate it a 8.0 out of 10. I may not reach for it seasonally as much as Sean John or Noir, but it performs better and smells better. Sadly in AZ there are only so many nights this can be worn.







yomiyomi 12/20/24 07:56

Armani Code EDT is nothing short of a signature masterpiece—a timeless and versatile fragrance that has left an indelible mark on the fragrance world. It suited every occasion and every age, garnering endless compliments and creating unforgettable impressions. Its discontinuation is both surprising and disheartening, representing a significant loss not only to its devoted fans but to the fragrance community as a whole.

When I purchased the new version in the updated bottle, I hoped it would preserve the magic of the original. While the new formula is pleasant and works well as a casual, everyday scent, it lacks the depth, elegance, and unmistakable allure that defined the original Armani Code EDT. To long-time admirers, the new version feels generic—a far cry from the sophistication we cherished.

The rapidly falling prices of Armani Code EDT reflect the fragrance community’s dissatisfaction with the new formula. Perfume enthusiasts no longer see the product as the masterpiece it once was. The original Armani Code stood shoulder-to-shoulder with iconic fragrances like Bleu de Chanel, Prada Pour Homme, Bvlgari Pour Homme, Le Male by Jean Paul Gaultier, YSL L’Homme, Drakkar Noir, and CK Eternity. Replacing it with something so fundamentally different feels like a missed opportunity.

Rather than letting Armani Code EDT disappear entirely, why not preserve its legacy by maintaining it as a classic icon in your lineup? Many other major brands have successfully kept their legendary fragrances available as heritage or legacy lines, providing enthusiasts with the opportunity to continue enjoying them.

This is more than just a sentimental appeal—it’s a sound business opportunity. Bringing back the original Armani Code EDT would be met with widespread enthusiasm from fragrance lovers worldwide, reigniting loyalty and interest in the Armani fragrance range.

Please reconsider discontinuing such an iconic creation. The fragrance community would be forever grateful to see this legend endure.
p.s. do not discontinue ACQUA DI GIÒ

Smellybutgood 12/18/23 21:39

Don't be diswayed by the negative reviews. This is a fantastic fragrance!

In the midst of all the chatter about Armani Code's reformulations, one might question if some critics truly experienced the original Armani Black Code, witnessed its first tweak, and now label pre-2023 formulations as subpar. (By the way, I own batches from 2004, 2010, and 2022—the 2004 one was my late father's. And no, that wasn't a typo. The OG was called Black Code, not Code.)

Could it be that some critics toss shade and negative reviews just to spice things up, hoping for unanimous nods?

Educate yourself. The name shifted in 2005 from Black Code to Armani Code, deemed "more appropriate" by De Lesquen, embodying "the ultimate code of seduction for men."

Yes, the 2004 Armani Black Code underwent a makeover around 2008ish, including a sneaky bottle change (comaband added). The juice had subtle shifts, but nothing to raise alarms. Fast forward to 2023, a new bottle design reminiscent of the Parfum version appears, sans the magnetic cap. Surprise—the juice inside has changed again. The deep, mysterious allure we cherished is replaced by a more blue-leaning scent, akin to Bleu De Chanel and its kin.

• Pre-2023 reformulation, is it a terrible fragrance? No, just not what we're accustomed to. My recent 2022 batch from the first reformulation smells great.
• Is it a carbon copy of Armani Code Black? No.
• Does it stink? Not at all.
• Does it resemble a completely different fragrance? Not even close.
• Does it vanish after two hours, as some claim? Definitely not. I get a solid 6 hours out of it.

Trust me, even with its reformulated quirks, Code still has something for the curious. It's still richer and darker than many similar scents out there. You can still pick up on the clever use of anise. Sure, it might have lost a bit of intensity, but it gained a more easygoing vibe, like Armani Code took a stroll on the beach and decided to lighten up.

Armani Code pre-2023 is still a fantastic fragrance, even with it's reformulation. Not all fragrances were intended to last 40 days and 40 nights people. It's suppose to last just long enough until sexy time.

Now back to your regular scheduled complaints.

Armani Code continues to be the dark horse in my 100+ collection, shedding light to fragrances from the 2000's with it's bold opening full of star anise and bergamot.

Sometimes, what I look for as my collection grows is uniqueness, and Armani Code is no exception: Take everything you know about fragrances with bergamot and lemon, now imagine something citrusy with a dark twist, elegant, smooth, out of the ordinary. Armani Code has you feeling like you are smelling something very special.

That deep blend of star anise, tobacco and leather really has you feeling like a million bucks. Often fragrances might have an issue with leaning too far on one side: Citrus or leather/dark. Code blends both aspects to perfection, outstanding perfumery here.

Longevity is above average for an EDT but I imagine buying myself the EDP soon.

Carlitos 01/25/23 16:30

The word "code" can stand for several meanings. As for the fragrance Armani Code, I dare say its best synonyms are "manners", "ethics" or even "etiquette". After this introduction, the epytome "boring" might also appear, but I assure you, this is not the case. Armani Code is a versatile and unobtrusive fragrance that is suitable for many everyday situations. As a rule, it is well received by neighbouring noses. It is also a "cautious" perfume, providing a certain freshness and greenness through the use of citrus and oily olive blossom, a certain sharpness through the use of star anise and tobacco, a certain sobriety through the use of gaiac wood and leather, and a certain sweetness through tonka bean. It really is an all-round fragrance that is good on many occasions but excels on none. It's not a front-runner, but it's better than most other fragrances for an educated man on his way to the office in any business metropolis.
Market-wise, the original Code has carved a place for itself as the "other" Armani after the more aquatic and successful Acqua di Giò pour Homme. It is elegant and classic and deserves much more attention than it has received so far. It justifies a better place than just being the brand's secondary reference as a men's fragrance. In my opinion, I even prefer to use it than its more famous aquatic brother.
Armani Code is a conservative, spicy-sweet fragrance that offers below-average performance for the fragrance type, a beautiful visual presentation and an undeniable ability to please ladies (but not girls). It opens, as usual with Armani, with efemerous citrus notes, later developing a more herbaceous phase with oily olive blossom accords spiced with star anise facets. It dries down woody and moderately sweet and leathery.
This perfume is a little "lost" on the perfumery shelves with so many competing offerings from the same brand. I would say that it is even underrated when competing with the numerous more bold Armani "Profumos", "Profondos" and "Absolutes". The fragrance DNA is distinctive, even if it doesn't really stand out due to its overall moderate accords and visceral good manners. Its lack of sales success has not persuaded any copycat brand to produce a clone fragrance. Jeanne En Provence has, however, produced an inexpensive similar perfume called Bois d'Olivier & Cade by Jeanne en Provence, which I also enjoy wearing. My wife likes both fragrances on me very much.

My opinion:
Since I first reviewed this fragrance a few years ago, the price became very attractive for an Armani offering. Besides being an above average dumb reach fragrance, it is also a good choice for mid-season elegant and formal occasions or for a meal with friends in a restaurant. It doesn't smell dated and I prefer it to other woody, sweet, formal fragrances in the same price range and also sold by fashion designers. I still don't think a blind purchase is justifiable, but it will be easy to test it in different perfumeries.

Music: Tanita Tikaram - "Good Tradition"

MustafaJ 09/18/23 13:18

Before the Bleu de Chanels, Sauvages, Dior Hommes, Laytons and Le Males, this was the king of modern mass appealing masculine scents.

With no prior experience or interest in fragrances, this was my first perfume purchase. The year was 2008, I had just started a corporate job in a new country, and while exploring the city, I came across this gem and thought to myself at the time that I must have just discovered the best perfume in the world, so I immediately bought it. It became my signature scent over the next 2 years. I wore it daily to the office, on business trips, nights out with friends, dates and everything else.

I felt nostalgia today which is why I wrote this review, and have also gone ahead and ordered a 10ml decant of Armani Code Parfum which I expect to be a refined version of this classic.

10/10

FragrantAl87 11/27/12 12:06

Ah, Code. People almost universally say, "mmm" when they smell it. Overworn, yes, just like ADG. But I will not let that skew my opinion of such a wonderfully rich and complex smell.

Opening: Woah. Lemon quickly makes a tasty opening to a bold variety of earthtones that jump out at your nose. Bright, but deep.

Sillage: Not overwhelming; very nice for an EDT with such a crisp citrus opening. Probably about 3-4 feet for the same number of hours depending on humidity and skin type.

Longevity: Quite good. Its on my clothes for a few days after a couple sprays. On my skin without moisturizer, 4-5 hours per application, I'd say.

Best for: Come on, its code, its like the duct tape of fragrances. Use it anywhere, anytime for anything, you'll get compliments.

Gripes: Overworn, and often oversprayed when it is worn. I hear "my boss smells like that", "my friend smells like that", "my ex smells like that", etc. Not unique anymore, sadly. Sometimes overshadows other good creations in the same genre simply because its Armani, also sad.

Overall: A classic, inspired creation. For the guy who's never worn cologne, there is nothing to fear here. Bold, deep and earthy. Your gf will like it, but she may say you smell like someone she knows :)

8.5/10

I absolutely love Armani Code. I first tried it in 2019, so I cannot comment on whether or not it is weaker than it used to be, etc. I mostly owned fresh/citrus/woody scents and started exploring different categories of frags, specifically something darker with a bit of mystery and romance. This seems to encapsulate everything I was looking for in that regard. It’s still fresh, with light hints of citrus, but the overall makeup is very dark and intensely masculine and alluring. It’s smooth and mysterious, it is my favorite scent for wearing at night, no matter the occasion. I simply adore the scent and it puts me in a fantastic mood. I work nights from my home office and I find certain scents help me focus, and this is in my top 3 favorites currently. It seems to be the perfect balance of light citrus, dark, smoky woods and deep leather with tobacco and a creamy/powdery touch. It’s like getting a fresh shave, at night, in a barbershop that just so happens to be in the middle of a deep, mystical forest with incense burning and cavemen tanning cowhides and rolling fresh cigars out of tree bark, and then you get a vanilla ice cream cone for dessert, and go slay an ancient beast under the moonlight.

Cassiano 10/28/14 13:13

The Giorgio Armani brand is synonymous with success in the entire world. But I dare say that, when it comes to men's fragrances, it seems that was always missing something, at least until the year 2004. In this year, was born one of the most celebrated fragrances of the past decade, making that men from all over the world searched for 1 bottle for their collections: Armani Black Code.

It was with this name that this oriental and spicy fragrance came on the market, bringing a mix of seductive and elegant notes concentrated in a dark and cylindrical bottle. In 2005, the name changed to Armani Code, but there is no official record of the real reason for the change. I've read reports of problems involving the term "Black" on the European market, but nothing confirmed.

The fragrance brings notes of bergamot and lemon, in the output; star anise, olive tree blossom, and guaiac wood, in the heart; tobacco, leather and tonka beans, in the base. At least on my skin, I don't see a single sign of the top notes. From the moment it touches the skin, there is a strong and sweet aroma. The star anise in this fragrance lacks the typical aroma of anise that sometimes recalls the smell of fennel. Here, the anise is more pungent, something closer to the licorice. The olive blossom note results in creamy, almost buttery nuances, while the guaiac wood has an incense-sandalwood aspect.

About 40 minutes later, we can notice a reduction in the sweet aspect and an increase of more elegant and strong nuances. The leather gives a dry tone, while the tobacco leaves the fragrance warmer and sensual. The tonka beans end the evolution with a slight aroma of almonds.

Many users feel the aroma of vanilla and some still complain of a certain medicinal smell. Worth trying on the skin. It's the kind of fragrance that exudes well, even though the concept is not the exposure, but the elegance. And has excellent durability.

Particularly, I just have a problem with this scent: I can't wear it for two days in a row, since something about it makes me tired, making impossible the idea of having it as my olfactory signature.

The bottle is dark but not black, as many think. It has a midnight blue color. Finally, it is worth saying that Armani Code won the Fifi Award for the fragrance of the year, in 2006, in the Men’s Luxe category.
